title: Google publishes guidance for Google-Agent: robots.txt is not the only gate
why: Expected: crawl access is set in robots.txt. Found: Google's new guidance says firewall and bot rules can block its agent even when the site is open to it.

drafts.text: Google published guidance for Google-Agent, the name for its AI agents that act for a user on websites (SEJ, 23 Nov). Robots.txt is one gate. A firewall or bot rule can still block the agent's follow-up requests.
thread: Mechanism: Google's guidance says to verify Google-Agent by user agent, by published IP range, and by Web Bot Auth signature where present. Rules that allow it must run before cloud-provider and bot-block rules. Rule order decides the outcome.
Limit: this is Search Engine Journal's summary of Google's documentation. The summary says Google does not name which products use Google-Agent. We have not tested any site against these rules.

Monday morning: check firewall and CDN logs for blocked requests with a Google-Agent user agent. Turn off CAPTCHA for agent traffic that passes Google's IP and signature checks. Our scan does not see WAF rules.

drafts.text:
Google published guidance this week on Google-Agent, the name for its AI agents that navigate sites and act for a user. The examples include adding products to a cart, making bookings and calling a site's APIs.

The part I keep coming back to: an agent can land on a page and still fail to finish. If a bot rule or firewall blocks the follow-up requests, the task stops there.

Robots.txt is one gate, not the only one. Our scanner reads robots.txt, sitemap, llms.txt and the homepage. It does not see firewall or CDN rules.

Method note: the source is Search Engine Journal's summary of Google's documentation, 23 Nov 2026. I have not read Google's page in full and have not tested any site against it. Confidence: medium on what the guidance says, low on how often it blocks anyone.
